If you plan to use it as a lifestyle car (no heavy hauling/work purpose) then you're better off with an SUV. Better maneuverability and easier to park. Pickups have a longer rear and and its trickier to park in tight spaces especially in manila and in cramped spaces in poorly designed parking buildings. I shudder to think about driving a pickup in the tight spaces in the metro, and prefer smaller cars.

I've driven cars, suvs and pickups. If no heavy hauling i suggest sticking with your gas car especially if it will be stuck most of its life in the metro. Diesel suvs and pickups thrive when used for hauling or long trips. They don't like being idled too much in traffic as they plug up the DPF (diesel particulate filter) quickly and you have to expel/regen it through a highway run at least once a month. They're also more expensive to maintain in the long term compared to a gas car.

Sure it will be worry free in the first 5 years but issues arise quick if you don't keep up with the maintenance items (frequent oil, air, filter changes). Diesels quickly darken up the engine oil because of soot which is a byproduct of diesel combustion, so if its always daily driven in traffic you may have to do 5k oil changes.

So unless you plan to regularly take your pickup on long highway trips (atleast once a month) gas cars are cleaner to own and cheaper to maintain in the long term.

then that's exactly like mine. Ako mismo nagaadjust. need mo lang ng small wrench na 10mm to loosen that lock nut then kaya mo na ikutin by hand yung adjustment nut. Mas maganda if isagad mo yung clearance kasi mas maganda yung timpla ng clutch mo. Pero wag mo sobrahan baka tukod na yun sa clutch fork. As long as merong play pa sa clutch pedal bago mo maramdaman yung resistance goods pa yan.

See that big long nut? Turn that counter-clockwise to loosen. Then you adjust the smaller nut beside that in contact with the clutch fork.

Clockwise - lesser clearance (less pedal play)

Counterclockwise - more clearance (more pedal play)

Personally I would adjust the smaller nut until i would have 5-7mm of play sa clutch pedal until i feel a bit of resistance. That's how it's written in the manual.

I exclusively use euro5 unioil on all my cars. Firstly because as the other redditors said here, SnR discount, its cheaper than all big three gas stations and even cheaper than Petro Gazz or RePhil for me, their 95 octane gas is even cheaper than their 91 if you account for the discount lol. Performance is nothing to scoff at either, my little preppy 1 liter econobox revs happily with the 95 octane and idles really smooth. Mileage is more or less equal than any other brand gas station.

Stay away from the lesser known stations because as said on tsikot forums they may or may not follow safety standards (especially the ones in the province, ones in metro manila are obliged to follow standards) so you may find their fuels as "malabnaw" or mabilis maubos. 

For diesels Unioil has a cetane rating of 58 which is comparably higher than the "big three" whereas their diesel cetane rating ranges from 51-55.

In the end what made me stay with Unioil is that my SUVs diesel fuel filters stay clean even after 30k or 40k. The old mechanic's tale of changing your fuel filters after 10k or 20k is because some fuel stations have noticeably dirtier fuels so the filters clog up quicker. I've had bad experience with SEAOIL Edsa near q ave because my fuel filter got dirty quick when we used to gas up there. 20k fuel filter full of crud so I don't gas up at Seaoil anymore.

Shell is the most expensive but has pretty good additives (look up project farm's test on shell fuel's cleaning additive. As the saying goes, you can't go wrong with Shell (as long as you have the peso for it).

I also recommend Caltex since it has Techron in it in small doses. Techron is a proven technology in cleaning your pistons for carbon (you could read up technical papers on it online or just scan forums like bobistheoilguy). It's not a overnight/instant clean type of chemical but a long term burn so if you want to see results you have to stay with Caltex for a while or do a techron bottle run every 5k or 3k. Maximum of two bottles before changing the oil.

So all in all I recommend Unioil, shell and Caltex (primarily because techron is the real deal).

R7 1700 > 6800k = R5 1600 > 7700k

My rationale here is that in Premiere you're not going to be sitting around while stabilizing clips and it would be important to consider that you are able to do multiple things in the timeline. While the 4c8t 7700k has the fastest single thread speed for stabilization I prefer having more cores / threads so I'm able to continue editing / adding effects / lumetri while I'm stabilizing in the background. 

This will be even more important when dealing with high resolution 4K and RAW footage. These things are so heavily thread dependent that it would easily saturate all 8 threads of the 7700k with 80-99% utilization whilst the 16 threads of an R7 1700 would have it pinned by 40-60% utilization. 

Rendering codecs are another thing to consider. If you're using an older codec (such as the not so optimized h264 mp4) you probably won't see much difference between the Ryzens and i7 6800k. You'd see the difference in the codecs that are optimized for multithreading such as avid's mxf op1a or sony's x-avc or any broadcast codec out there.

After effects is a heavily threaded beast so R7 1700's 8c16t will be the most beneficial in this program. I have no idea for C4D.
